title: Coulomb's Law: The Inverse-Square Tug
topic: Coulomb's law — F = k·q₁q₂/r²; force scales with the product of charges and the inverse square of distance; like repels, opposite attracts

beats.narration: Two charges in empty space — what does each one feel from the other?

elements.content: Manimo bobs in centre-screen
Two charges, nothing else — what tugs them?

beats.narration: Place a positive charge here and another positive charge there. The line between them is the line of force. Like signs push apart; opposite signs pull together.

elements.content: Left charge q₁ — amber circle on the horizontal axis
+q₁ inside left charge
Right charge q₂ — amber circle to the right
+q₂ inside right charge
Dashed line between the two charges showing the line of force
r distance label centred above the line
Repulsive force arrow on each charge — pointing outward (left charge pushes left, right charge pushes right)
like repels — opposite would attract

beats.narration: The strength of that push or pull follows Coulomb's law: F equals k times q one q two divided by r squared. Three knobs — the two charges and the distance.

elements.content: F = k · q₁q₂ / r²
elements.position: centre, large serif italic amber payoff

elements.content: k ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² — Coulomb's constant
double a charge → force doubles; double the distance → force quarters

beats.narration: Watch what the inverse square does. As we slide the second charge away, the force does not just fall — it falls fast. Twice the distance, one quarter the force.

elements.content: Anchored left charge at fixed x
Right charge whose x is swept from r=80 (close) out to r=320 over the beat
Force arrow on the right charge whose length scales as 1/r² in real time as the charge slides
F vs r axes below the diagram, F on the vertical, r on the horizontal
F = k/r² curve traced incrementally — the dot tracks the swept charge's position so the curve grows as the charge slides
Marker dot on the curve at the current (r, F) — moves with the swept charge
twice the distance → one quarter the force

beats.narration: Same shape as Newton's gravity, but stronger by far — and signed. Charges can pull or push; mass only ever pulls.

elements.content: Same shape as gravity — but stronger, and signed.
Charges push or pull. Mass only ever pulls.
(electricity is gravity's louder, two-faced cousin)
